phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Ra. These are the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom
phrases.explanation: The three separate letters open several chapters, and early commentators differed over them, with many leaving their exact meaning to Allah while still treating them as part of the revelation. What follows is clear, namely that these are verses of a Book described as wise. Wisdom points to firm construction and true judgment, so the reader is prepared for speech that decides matters rather than merely decorating them.

phrases.translation: Is it astonishing to people that We have sent revelation to a man from among themselves,
phrases.explanation: Wonder at a human messenger becomes the first objection answered. Revelation reaching one man from among his own people seemed ordinary in form, yet that nearness is part of the mercy, since he speaks their language and shares their condition. The question invites hearers to notice the assumption underneath, namely that guidance should arrive detached from ordinary humanity before it can be trusted.

phrases.translation: ˹instructing him,˺ “Warn humanity and give good news to the believers that they will have an honourable status with their Lord.”?
phrases.explanation: The messenger task is stated in two movements, warning humanity at large and giving good news to believers. An honourable status with their Lord renders an expression about a firm footing of truth, explained as a good place earned through earlier sincere deeds. Warning and glad news are held together from the start, so the message is neither threat alone nor comfort without accountability.

phrases.translation: Yet the disbelievers said, “Indeed, this ˹man˺ is clearly a magician!”
phrases.explanation: Calling him a magician explains away the power of the speech without examining its content. Magic was a convenient label when words divided families, unsettled customs, and moved hearts in ways opponents could not control. Clear adds confidence they did not possess in evidence. The verse exposes a familiar move, where naming a speaker replaces answering what the speaker actually says.

phrases.translation: Surely your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then established Himself on the Throne, conducting every affair.
phrases.explanation: Creation in six Days places heavens and earth inside a measured divine act rather than accident or rival powers. Early readers understood these Days by a measure known to Allah, the important point here being ordered creation followed by sovereign rule. Established on the Throne and conducting every affair join kingship with continuing management, so the Maker is not absent from what He made.

phrases.translation: None can intercede except by His permission. That is Allah—your Lord, so worship Him ˹alone˺. Will you not then be mindful
phrases.explanation: No intercession works outside permission, which closes the hope that other beings can pressure or bypass the Lord described. That is Allah gathers creation, rule, and permission into one identity before the command to worship Him alone. Will you not be mindful turns doctrine into reflection. The verse argues that remembrance should naturally follow once power and care are seen in the same hands.

phrases.translation: To Him is your return all together. Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true.
phrases.explanation: Return all together gives creation a destination and removes the idea that anyone exits the story at death. The promise of Allah being true answers doubt with reliability rather than with a schedule. Gathering everyone also levels worldly rank, because rulers and followers travel toward the same appointment. The opening of the verse sets resurrection inside a promise rather than a threat alone.

phrases.translation: Indeed, He originates the creation then resurrects it so that He may justly reward those who believe and do good.
phrases.explanation: The One who originates creation can also return it, an argument repeated whenever resurrection is doubted. Rewarding believers who do good justly shows purpose in the return, since lives of faith and action are not left unpaid or confused with their opposite. Belief and good deeds stay joined. The second creation therefore has a moral aim, not only a display of power.

phrases.translation: But those who disbelieve will have a boiling drink and a painful punishment for their disbelief
phrases.explanation: Boiling drink and painful punishment answer disbelief with images of intense discomfort. A drink should relieve thirst, so making it scald turns expectation inside out. The punishment is tied to what they disbelieved rather than presented as random cruelty. By placing reward and penalty in the same verse, the return becomes a sorting of lives rather than a uniform ending.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light,
phrases.explanation: The sun is given blazing radiance and the moon a gentler light, a distinction everyday eyes already recognise. One rules the working day while the other marks nights, travel, and worship. By assigning both to Allah design, the verse removes them from worship as independent powers. Familiar lights become servants inside an order rather than gods above it.

phrases.translation: with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺.
phrases.explanation: Moon phases are precisely arranged so people can count years and measure time for contracts, fasting, pilgrimage, planting, and debt. A changing shape in the sky becomes a public calendar available to rich and poor alike. Calculation here is practical mercy, since shared time allows a society to coordinate duties. The verse joins astronomy to daily obedience without making the sky an object of awe alone.

phrases.translation: Allah did not create all this except for a purpose.
phrases.explanation: All this was created only in truth, meaning with right purpose rather than in play. The word answers any sense that the heavens are decoration over a meaningless earth. Purpose in the larger order prepares the reader for purpose in human life and resurrection. If moons run by measure, the lives under them are unlikely to be abandoned to chance.

phrases.translation: He makes the signs clear for people of knowledge
phrases.explanation: Signs are explained for people who know, a description earned by attention rather than birth. Knowledge in this setting means reading a regular world as evidence of its Maker, then allowing that evidence to direct worship. The same sky hangs over everyone, yet only some gather its lesson. The verse makes learning an act of reverence that begins with looking carefully.

phrases.translation: Surely in the alternation of the day and the night, and in all that Allah has created in the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: Alternation of night and day is a sign repeated so often that familiarity can hide it. Sleep and work, heat and coolness, visibility and rest all depend on a rhythm nobody in the audience controls. Adding everything in heavens and earth widens the evidence beyond one cycle. The verse asks the reader to treat ordinary dependable order as a summons rather than background.

phrases.translation: there are truly signs for those mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: Mindful people receive these things as signs because fear of Allah keeps the eyes spiritually awake. The same sunrise can start a market day or remind a heart of resurrection after the small death of sleep. Mindfulness does not add new objects to the world. It changes the quality of attention brought to objects already present every morning and night.

phrases.translation: Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, being pleased and content with this worldly life, and who are heedless of Our signs
phrases.explanation: Not expecting to meet Allah reshapes desire until this world feels sufficient. Pleasure and contentment here describe a settled satisfaction that no longer asks whether another life will judge this one. Heedlessness of signs follows, since evidence is unwelcome when it interrupts comfort. The verse works as the opening half of a sentence completed next, so its weight gathers before the destination is named.

phrases.translation: they will have the Fire as a home because of what they have committed
phrases.explanation: The Fire as home completes the portrait of people satisfied with a temporary residence. Home implies settling rather than passing through, a grim answer to those who made worldly life their final address. Because of what they earned ties the end to accumulated choices, not to a single mistaken opinion. Contentment without expectation finally becomes a dwelling nobody would choose if seen clearly.

phrases.translation: Surely those who believe and do good, their Lord will guide them ˹to Paradise˺ through their faith,
phrases.explanation: Guidance by faith presents belief as a light that carries its people beyond death. Their Lord guides them because of faith joined with good works, suggesting that trust in life becomes direction in the next world. The road to Paradise is not improvised at the end. It grows from the orientation already chosen when signs were read with humility rather than ignored.

phrases.translation: rivers will flow under their feet in the Gardens of Bliss
phrases.explanation: Rivers under their feet in Gardens of Bliss answer effort with rest and beauty. Bliss names a state free from the anxieties that attach to worldly pleasure, including loss and decay. Flowing water again suits a hearer formed by dry land and difficult travel. The verse keeps reward concrete while rooting it in guidance, so Paradise is both place and relationship.

phrases.translation: in which their prayer will be, “Glory be to You, O Allah!”
phrases.explanation: Their prayer in Paradise begins with glory to Allah, suggesting that worship continues as joy rather than burden. Words once used in struggle and need become the natural language of satisfaction. Early explanations pictured requests themselves turning into glorification as wishes were granted. The scene tells readers that nearness to Allah is part of bliss, not a duty added outside it.

phrases.translation: and their greeting will be, “Peace!” and their closing prayer will be, “All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds!”
phrases.explanation: Peace as greeting means every encounter carries safety, while praise to the Lord of all worlds closes their speech. A society is imagined where conversation never wounds and gratitude never runs out. The closing praise also echoes the opening of the Quran, framing existence from first instruction to final home. Their last word is not about themselves but about the Lord who brought them there.

phrases.translation: If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed.
phrases.explanation: If evil were hastened the way people hasten after good, their term would already have ended. Human beings pray in anger, curse themselves and families, and demand immediate outcomes they would not survive if answered literally. Delay therefore appears as mercy hidden inside apparent silence. The verse corrects impatience by showing that instant response is not always kindness, especially when the request grows from rage.

phrases.translation: But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their defiance
phrases.explanation: Those who do not expect the meeting are left to wander in transgression, a punishment that can look like freedom for a long time. Wandering blindly suggests movement without arrival, where appetite chooses each next road. Divine leaving follows repeated human refusal in the moral pattern of the passage. Extra time can become either a door to return or deeper weather for a hardened direction.

phrases.translation: Whenever someone is touched by hardship, they cry out to Us, whether lying on their side, sitting, or standing.
phrases.explanation: Hardship makes a person call on Allah from every posture, lying, sitting, and standing, because pain removes the feeling of self sufficiency. The verse notices behaviour anyone can test in illness, danger, or loss. Sincerity in crisis proves that the heart already knows where help lies. Trouble becomes an unwilling teacher, stripping away the partners and plans that normally share our confidence.

phrases.translation: But when We relieve their hardship, they return to their old ways as if they had never cried to Us to remove any hardship!
phrases.explanation: Relief often restores the old road so completely that the crisis prayer seems never to have happened. Passing on as if untouched is the moral failure, since gratitude should have converted emergency faith into steady obedience. Forgetting here is active rather than accidental. Ease asks whether the lesson survived the removal of pain, and many biographies in the chapter will answer through conduct.

phrases.translation: This is how the misdeeds of the transgressors have been made appealing to them
phrases.explanation: Misdeeds made appealing explains how a person can return to a road already exposed as empty. Old habits recover their shine once fear fades, especially when companions and desires decorate them again. Transgressors are those who cross the limit after seeing it clearly. The verse warns readers between illnesses and dangers, when gratitude usually decides whether relief becomes worship or merely recovery.

phrases.translation: We surely destroyed ˹other˺ peoples before you when they did wrong,
phrases.explanation: Destroyed peoples before this audience establish that warnings have historical outcomes. Wrongdoing is named as the condition when destruction came, not weakness or bad fortune alone. The verse speaks to Meccan hearers who knew ruins and stories of earlier nations through travel and report. History becomes a nearby evidence, because the roads of trade carried both merchandise and memory.

phrases.translation: and their messengers came to them with clear proofs but they would not believe!
phrases.explanation: Messengers came with clear proofs, so refusal cannot be blamed on obscure teaching. They were not going to believe describes settled resistance after evidence, the point where argument becomes loyalty to a chosen position. Clarity increases responsibility because a person can no longer call rejection a shortage of light. The repeated pattern turns ancient stories into a mirror held before present hearers.

phrases.translation: This is how We reward the wicked people
phrases.explanation: Rewarding the guilty in this manner presents destruction as a fitting requital rather than a random disaster. Guilty gathers wrongdoing, proof, and persistence into one description. The verse is severe, yet its logic still gives hearers time to choose a different ending. A warning that names the past honestly is itself a mercy to people not yet at the end.

phrases.translation: Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act
phrases.explanation: Successors in the land inherit an examination along with houses, fields, and roads. To see how you act expresses the public outcome of choices already known to Allah. The present generation stands where ruined peoples once stood, with their chance still open. Inheritance therefore carries a question rather than a guarantee, because occupying the land proves nothing about deserving to remain in it.

phrases.translation: When Our clear revelations are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say ˹to the Prophet˺,
phrases.explanation: Clear revelations produce a consumer request from people who do not expect the meeting. Recitation itself is not the problem for them, since they understand enough to dislike its judgments. Their objection begins when the message refuses to praise their customs or soften resurrection and idolatry. The verse sets the scene with clarity on one side and negotiation on the other.

phrases.translation: “Bring us a different Quran or make some changes in it.”
phrases.explanation: Bring another Quran or change this one asks revelation to be redesigned around audience comfort. The demand can sound open minded while actually setting the listener as editor over God. A changed book that approved their desires would no longer function as guidance. The verse exposes the difference between asking for understanding and asking for a message customised in advance.

phrases.translation: Say ˹to them˺, “It is not for me to change it on my own.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet answer removes personal authorship from the dispute. It is not for him to alter revelation from himself, which protects both his honesty and the source of the words. A messenger who could edit under pressure would become another tribal negotiator. Refusal here is therefore not stubbornness but fidelity to a trust, since the speech he delivers is not his property.

phrases.translation: I only follow what is revealed to me. I fear, if I were to disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.”
phrases.explanation: Following only what is revealed makes obedience the Prophet method before it becomes his instruction to others. Fear of disobeying his Lord and of a tremendous Day gives his refusal emotional depth. He does not stand above the warning he announces. The verse also answers the magician charge indirectly, because a self serving inventor would likely accept an edit that bought applause.

phrases.translation: Say, “Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you.
phrases.explanation: Had Allah willed otherwise, the Quran would not have been recited or made known through him at all. The argument shifts attention from audience demand to divine choice, because revelation exists by permission rather than human pressure. A messenger under command cannot be treated as an author shopping for approval. The sentence also humbles the reciter, who claims no independent power over the event.

phrases.translation: I had lived my whole life among you before this ˹revelation˺. Do you not understand?”
phrases.explanation: Living a whole life among them before revelation gives the audience a biography to examine. For forty years they had known his honesty, habits, and lack of literary ambition in the reports surrounding the passage. Do you not understand asks them to connect that record with the sudden charge of invention. Character evidence does not replace revelation, yet it makes careless accusation harder to sustain.

phrases.translation: Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations? Indeed, the wicked will never succeed
phrases.explanation: Fabricating a lie against Allah and denying His signs are placed together as supreme wrongdoing. One invents false religion, while the other rejects true guidance when it arrives. Wicked people never truly succeed even if a lie wins followers or a denial protects status for a while. The verse measures success at the final return, where borrowed authority and rejected proof both lose their shelter.

phrases.translation: They worship besides Allah others who can neither harm nor benefit them, and say, “These are our intercessors with Allah.”
phrases.explanation: Objects that neither harm nor benefit are worshipped and then described as intercessors. The contradiction sits inside the practice, since a powerless being is asked to influence the All Powerful. Intercession becomes a hopeful story told to preserve inherited devotion. The verse does not deny intercession by Allah permission elsewhere. It denies that helpless partners possess a share they can promise on their own.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Are you informing Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or the earth?
phrases.explanation: Are you informing Allah of something He does not know turns their theology into an absurd report. If such partners and rights existed anywhere in heavens or earth, the Knower of both would not need worshippers to announce them. The question exposes invention dressed as information. It also protects inquiry, because claims about unseen authority require a source stronger than custom and desire.

phrases.translation: Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him˺!”
phrases.explanation: Glorified and Exalted closes the argument by raising Allah far above the partners described. People may associate others in speech and ritual, yet association does not create a real division in divinity. The sentence cleans the discussion after the imagined intercessors have been examined. Worship returns to proportion when the mind remembers that a partner who needs worshippers cannot stand beside the Lord who needs nothing.

phrases.translation: Humanity was once nothing but a single community ˹of believers˺, but then they differed.
phrases.explanation: Humanity begins in the passage as one community before difference enters. Early commentators explained the original unity in more than one way, including a period upon truth before disputes spread. The shared point is that division is a later human condition rather than the first word of the story. Present religious conflict therefore needs explanation and judgment, not passive acceptance as nature.

phrases.translation: Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled ˹at once˺
phrases.explanation: A prior decree delays the settling of differences until an appointed time. Without that word, every dispute might have been decided immediately when it appeared. Delay gives space for messengers, argument, repentance, and the slow exposure of motives. It also warns readers not to mistake postponement for indifference, since a matter can be scheduled without being forgotten.

phrases.translation: They ask, “Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?”
phrases.explanation: Why is no sign sent down means no additional sign of the kind they demand. The Quran itself and the signs already described are treated as insufficient because the request often functions as delay. A spectator miracle can become another item to negotiate rather than a door to obedience. The verse notices that appetite for wonders may grow precisely where willingness to submit is absent.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹The knowledge of˺ the unseen is with Allah alone.
phrases.explanation: The unseen belongs to Allah alone, so its timing and form are not managed by the Prophet or his audience. This answer limits prophetic authority in a healthy direction, because even the messenger waits for what God chooses to disclose. Human curiosity does not become a schedule for heaven. The sentence also protects faith from turning into a market where each new demand raises the price.

phrases.translation: So wait! I too am waiting with you.”
phrases.explanation: So wait places both sides under a future disclosure. The Prophet waits with them, not as an equal in guilt but as a servant who trusts the outcome. Waiting here is firm rather than idle, because the message continues while the requested spectacle is refused. The verse teaches that patience can be an answer when more evidence would only feed a refusal already chosen.

phrases.translation: When We give people a taste of mercy after being afflicted with a hardship, they swiftly devise plots against Our revelations!
phrases.explanation: Mercy after hardship should produce gratitude, yet some people quickly plot against the revelations once pressure lifts. Taste suggests a sample of relief rather than permanent security, making the speed of the turn more striking. Plotting can include mockery, distortion, and searching for contradictions to neutralise the message. The verse returns to the cycle from verse twelve and gives it a sharper edge.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah is swifter in devising ˹punishment˺. Surely Our messenger-angels record whatever you devise.”
phrases.explanation: Allah swifter in planning answers human schemes with a greater knowledge of outcomes. Recorded by messenger angels means the plots are not lost in the noise of conversation after relief. Writing creates accountability for words crafted in private rooms and public gatherings alike. The reply removes the comfort of cleverness, because speed in devising an argument is not the same as escaping its record.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who enables you to travel through land and sea.
phrases.explanation: Travel by land and sea begins as a divine enablement before any storm appears. Roads, animals, winds, ships, and human skill all operate inside capacities Allah created. Starting here prevents gratitude from being reduced to rescue alone. Ordinary safe movement is already a gift, and the coming scene will test whether people recognise the Giver when the gift becomes fragile.

phrases.translation: And it so happens that you are on ships, sailing with a favourable wind, to the passengers’ delight.
phrases.explanation: A favourable wind and delighted passengers create the calm half of the parable. Competent sailing and pleasant weather can make a vessel feel like a small controlled world. Delight is not condemned by itself. It becomes revealing only when the following danger shows how quickly confidence had forgotten its limits. The verse slows down at happiness so the reader can enter the scene honestly.

phrases.translation: Suddenly, the ships are overcome by a gale wind and those on board are overwhelmed by waves from every side, and they assume they are doomed.
phrases.explanation: Gale and waves from every side remove the exits one by one. To assume they are surrounded or doomed means the imagination reaches the end before the body does. Skilled sailors still face a scale that mocks planning. The storm works as a concentrated version of every crisis in the chapter, where human arrangements remain real yet suddenly stand under a greater power.

phrases.translation: They cry out to Allah ˹alone˺ in sincere devotion, “If You save us from this, we will certainly be grateful.”
phrases.explanation: In sincere devotion they call on Allah alone and promise gratitude if saved. Crisis strips partner worship down to instinct, because idols and intercessors are forgotten when waves rise. The promise sounds complete in the moment, and it may even be emotionally true. Its weakness lies in duration. The verse sets a vow inside terror so the next verse can examine post rescue memory.

phrases.translation: But as soon as He rescues them, they transgress in the land unjustly.
phrases.explanation: As soon as rescue arrives, transgression resumes on land with unjust speed. Dry ground restores appetite, status games, and the feeling that promises belonged to another world. The failure is not ingratitude as a mood only. It becomes action against others, showing that a forgotten vow soon affects neighbours as well as the soul that made it.

phrases.translation: O humanity! Your transgression is only against your own souls.
phrases.explanation: Your transgression is against your own souls relocates the damage. People may imagine that wrongdoing mainly outwits rivals or escapes God, yet the first territory harmed is the self that learns corruption. Calling out to humanity widens the ship scene into a general law. Each unjust gain deposits its cost inside the person who will later need an undamaged soul.

phrases.translation: ˹There is only˺ brief enjoyment in this worldly life, then to Us is your return,
phrases.explanation: Brief enjoyment measures worldly success by duration rather than intensity. A pleasure can feel total while it lasts and still be brief beside return to Allah. Then to Us returns the sailors to the same destination as every settled land dweller. The verse refuses to let rescue become exemption from judgment, because surviving a storm only extends the journey toward an account.

phrases.translation: and then We will inform you of what you used to do
phrases.explanation: We will inform you means deeds will be told back with exact knowledge. The phrase covers promises made at sea and conduct resumed on shore in one record. Self storytelling often separates crisis identity from ordinary identity, as if two different people acted. Final information joins them again. The verse therefore turns memory into a moral duty long before the last telling arrives.

phrases.translation: The life of this world is just like rain We send down from the sky,
phrases.explanation: Worldly life is compared to rain because its growth begins as a gift from above rather than a human invention. Rain quickly changes colourless land into movement, food, and hope. The comparison starts with generosity, not contempt for the world. It asks readers to admire the process accurately while remembering the seasons that govern every green thing.

phrases.translation: producing a mixture of plants which humans and animals consume.
phrases.explanation: Mixed plants eaten by people and animals widen the picture into a whole local economy. Gardens, fodder, markets, milk, and meat all depend on the same fall of water. Human civilisation sits inside vegetation more than pride usually admits. By drawing animals into the scene, the verse reminds powerful readers that their life rests on fragile growth shared with creatures below their notice.

phrases.translation: Then just as the earth looks its best, perfectly beautified, and its people think they have full control over it,
phrases.explanation: Earth at its best and people thinking they control it marks the psychological peak of the parable. Beauty creates confidence, and confidence matures into an illusion of ownership over rain, soil, and future harvests. Perfectly adorned suggests a bride like display in classical imagery, at the moment of maximum charm. The danger is not enjoying the field. It is forgetting how recently it was dust.

phrases.translation: there comes to it Our command by night or by day,
phrases.explanation: Our command arrives by night or day, so no schedule of human vigilance can bargain with it. Blight, flood, locusts, storm, or sudden political ruin can enter fields and lives under the same principle. The command matters more than the instrument. Because timing belongs to Allah, the feeling of full control is exposed as a story told during a pleasant season.

phrases.translation: so We mow it down as if it never flourished yesterday!
phrases.explanation: Mown down as if it never flourished yesterday compresses a lifetime of growth into stubble. The recent past feels unreal once beauty vanishes, which is exactly how fortunes, bodies, and reputations can turn. Yesterday stresses speed, because no long decline is needed for the lesson. The parable does not say joy was fake. It says permanence was the false part.

phrases.translation: This is how We make the signs clear for people who reflect
phrases.explanation: People who reflect receive the signs because parables require a mind willing to travel from image to life. Rain and harvest are familiar enough to pass without thought. Reflection connects the field outside town with the reader body, wealth, and plans. The verse ends by making contemplation a form of knowledge, since the deepest evidence often begins in ordinary sight.

phrases.translation: And Allah invites ˹all˺ to the Home of Peace and guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: The Home of Peace answers the mown field with a dwelling that does not wither. Allah invites to it, which makes Paradise a call before it is a reward, while guidance to the Straight Path remains His gift to whom He wills. Peace describes safety from death, sorrow, enmity, and decay. After seasons of growth and cutting, the invitation points beyond seasonal life altogether.

phrases.translation: Those who do good will have the finest reward and ˹even˺ more.
phrases.explanation: The finest reward and even more promise generosity beyond exact equivalence for those who do good beautifully. More was explained by many early reports as looking toward Allah, the greatest addition beyond Paradise itself, while the wording still honours every lesser increase. Goodness receives abundance rather than a wage grudgingly counted. The verse encourages excellence by showing a Lord who outgives the deed.

phrases.translation: Neither gloom nor disgrace will cover their faces. It is they who will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: No gloom or disgrace on faces makes inner honour visible. Faces carry the public weather of the soul, and dust or humiliation would signal loss before a word was spoken. Residents of Paradise forever completes their safety with permanence. The line answers the mown field directly, because these people settle in a place where beauty is not waiting for a command to vanish.

phrases.translation: As for those who commit evil, the reward of an evil deed is its equivalent.
phrases.explanation: Evil is repaid with its equivalent, setting a measured limit on punishment in contrast with multiplied reward. Divine generosity tips the scales toward goodness, while justice prevents evil from escaping its own measure. Equivalence matters because the verse does not describe excess in return. A life may however accumulate many evil deeds, making a just measure heavy through repetition rather than inflation.

phrases.translation: Humiliation will cover them—with no one to protect them from Allah—as if their faces were covered with patches of the night’s deep darkness.
phrases.explanation: Humiliation covering faces like pieces of deep night makes disgrace visible as darkness pasted over identity. No protector from Allah returns to the failed intercessor theme, because the partners invoked in life cannot intervene now. Night patches suggest both gloom and fragmentation, as if a face can no longer gather light. The picture judges inward choices through outward appearance.

phrases.translation: It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: Residents of the Fire forever mirrors the previous verse with terrible symmetry. Residence again means settling, only now the home chosen through persistent evil cannot be exchanged. Forever refuses the imagination that punishment is a short embarrassment after a long life of appetite. The parallel structure forces the reader to see two permanences growing from two patterns of earthly conduct.

phrases.translation: ˹Consider˺ the Day We will gather them all together then say to those who associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺,
phrases.explanation: Gathering everyone together introduces a courtroom scene for those who associated partners with Allah. The command will be addressed in public, where private theories about intercession can no longer hide behind custom. Together also means worshippers and worshipped objects meet in one place. The verse uses future staging to test present claims, asking whether a partner can speak when the gathering finally arrives.

phrases.translation: “Stay in your places—you and your associate-gods.”
phrases.explanation: Stay in your places freezes movement before separation begins. You and your partners places the claimed alliance side by side under command, not under the worshippers control. Suspense is part of the exposure, since the next sentence will divide what devotion had joined. The scene teaches in advance that nearness invented through ritual cannot survive an order from the true Master.

phrases.translation: We will separate them from each other, and their associate-gods will say, “It was not us that you worshipped
phrases.explanation: Separation arrives and the partners deny that the worship was truly directed to them. Idols, angels, righteous figures, or beings falsely invoked are imagined clearing themselves of the contract made in their names. Their speech matters whether read as literal future utterance or as the truth made plain. Devotion addressed through invention discovers that its intended helpers never agreed to the role.

phrases.translation: Allah is sufficient as a Witness between each of us that we were totally unaware of your worship.”
phrases.explanation: Allah as sufficient Witness ends the partners defence with a courtroom appeal. They claim complete unawareness of the worship offered to them, which removes both knowledge and consent from the imagined partnership. Sufficiency means no further witness can rescue the claim once God testifies to the facts. The verse leaves worshippers alone with a devotion whose supposed recipients deny ever receiving it.

phrases.translation: Then and there every soul will face ˹the consequences of˺ what it had done.
phrases.explanation: Then and there gives judgment a location in experience, where each soul tests what it sent ahead. Face the consequences renders an idea of tasting or examining former deeds when they can no longer be revised. A person meets the biography as an environment rather than a story told by others. The verse brings the gathering down from crowds to the individual soul.

phrases.translation: They all will be returned to Allah—their True Master. And whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them
phrases.explanation: Return to Allah as True Master strips mastery from every fabricated god. True contrasts with titles that functioned socially while never possessing power at the decisive moment. Whatever they invented will stray away or vanish, leaving the worshipper without support. The verse closes the intercessor argument with geography, because all roads end at one Master and the invented companions are no longer on the road.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Who provides for you from heaven and earth?
phrases.explanation: The argument begins with provision from heaven and earth, rain above and crops, water, and minerals below. Instead of opening with an abstract definition of God, the question gathers the sources of a daily meal. Such provision is too broad and continuous to be managed by a carved partner. The hearer is led from breakfast and rainfall toward lordship by a road already recognised.

phrases.translation: Who owns ˹your˺ hearing and sight? Who brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living?
phrases.explanation: Hearing and sight move the question from the landscape into the body, asking who owns the two gates of knowledge. Living from dead and dead from living covers seed and soil, birth and decay, and the larger rhythm of generations. These processes happen near enough to be undeniable yet remain far beyond human manufacture. The partner gods are tested against functions they never claimed to perform.

phrases.translation: And who conducts every affair?” They will ˹surely˺ say, “Allah.”
phrases.explanation: They will say Allah records the expected answer before the next question is asked. Meccan polytheism already accepted a supreme Creator while reserving worship and nearness for lesser beings. Conducting every affair leaves no independent department for partners to administer. The argument therefore works from shared ground, because the dispute concerns worship owed to the Lord they already name in creation.

phrases.translation: Say, “Will you not then fear ˹Him˺
phrases.explanation: Will you not then fear Him draws the practical conclusion their admission should produce. Fear here means guarding against disobedience to the Provider, Owner, and Manager just acknowledged. A gap opens between a correct answer in argument and a divided life in practice. The short sentence asks why tongues can identify the Lord accurately while hands still build altars to others.

phrases.translation: That is Allah—your True Lord. So what is beyond the truth except falsehood?
phrases.explanation: That is Allah gathers the admissions into the title True Lord. Once truth is identified, what remains beyond it is called error rather than a second respectable road. The verse uses a boundary line instead of endlessly reopening settled premises. If provision, senses, life, death, and management all point one way, turning elsewhere needs a reason stronger than habit.

phrases.translation: How can you then be turned away?”
phrases.explanation: How are you turned away asks about the force that rotates a person after recognition. A passive shape suits social pressure, appetite, and inherited fear working on the mind until the clear answer feels strange. Delusion is not always a lack of data. It can be a movement away from data already accepted. The verse leaves hearers to locate the hand turning them.

phrases.translation: And so your Lord’s decree has been proven true against the rebellious—that they will never believe
phrases.explanation: The word of the Lord proves true against those who persist in rebellion and therefore will not believe. Early commentators connected such decrees with people whose repeated refusal reaches a settled end known to Allah. The verse should not be used to guess the hidden fate of neighbours. Its function in the argument is to explain obstinacy that survives premises, parables, history, and direct questions without softening.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Can any of your associate-gods originate creation and then resurrect it?”
phrases.explanation: Originating creation and returning it makes resurrection the test case for partner gods. A being that cannot begin life cannot credibly promise to restore it after decay. The question assumes the audience already assigns first creation to Allah, so the second act should be easier to accept. Denial of resurrection therefore struggles against the very power their creation belief already confesses.

phrases.translation: Say, “˹Only˺ Allah originates creation and then resurrects it. How can you then be deluded ˹from the truth˺?”
phrases.explanation: Only Allah begins and returns creation, after which delusion names the movement away from that logic. Bones and dust look final to eyes trained on graves, yet the first emergence from nothing was no smaller problem. Repetition of the start shows the argument resting on one point from several sides. If a partner cannot create, devotion directed there is separated from the power that gives life.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Can any of your associate-gods guide to the truth?”
phrases.explanation: Guidance to truth shifts the test from cosmic power to direction. A god worth following should be able to show the road, not merely receive offerings along roads chosen by priests or ancestors. The question exposes a gap between reverence and function. An object carried from place to place cannot carry its worshippers toward truth in return.

phrases.translation: Say, “˹Only˺ Allah guides to the truth.” Who then is more worthy to be followed:
phrases.explanation: Only Allah guides to truth states the positive side before comparison begins. Guidance includes revelation, signs in creation, moral clarity, and the inner opening by which a person accepts what is shown. The sentence prepares a courtroom choice about worthiness to be followed. Once the functions are separated, courtesy toward inherited partners cannot make the comparison equal without denying the evidence just named.

phrases.translation: the One Who guides to the truth or those who cannot find the way unless guided?
phrases.explanation: The One who guides is set against beings that cannot find the way unless they are guided. Needing guidance is not shameful for a creature, yet it disqualifies a creature from being worshipped as lord. The audience would not choose a lost guide for a desert crossing while rejecting one who knows every well. The verse asks religion to obey the same plain standard used in travel.

phrases.translation: What is the matter with you? How do you judge
phrases.explanation: What is the matter with you and how do you judge turn from the objects to the judges. Faulty comparison requires a faulty scale, and here the scale gives inherited beings credit for powers they lack. The questions sound exasperated because the premises are simple. By naming judgment itself, the verse suggests that reform may need new criteria before new evidence can be recognised.

phrases.translation: Most of them follow nothing but ˹inherited˺ assumptions. ˹And˺ surely assumptions can in no way replace the truth.
phrases.explanation: Assumption here means inherited conjecture treated as knowledge about gods, intercession, and the unseen. It can organise festivals and family loyalty while still offering nothing against truth in the decisive sense. A guess may help a traveller choose a path under uncertainty, yet it cannot create a partner beside Allah. The verse attacks confidence without foundation rather than ordinary human reasoning.

phrases.translation: Allah is indeed All-Knowing of what they do
phrases.explanation: Allah knows what they do closes the critique with exact awareness. Conjecture is not judged only as an opinion in the head, because it generates worship, spending, vows, and social pressure. Deeds built on a guess still enter the record. The sentence also comforts the Prophet, since majority opinion is visible to God with its sources and does not become truth by numbers.

phrases.translation: It is not ˹possible˺ for this Quran to have been produced by anyone other than Allah.
phrases.explanation: This Quran could not be produced from other than Allah answers the fabrication charge at the level of origin. In the passage, the claim rests on coherence, knowledge, guidance, and the known life of the man reciting it. A borrowed or invented book would carry a different relationship to its maker. The verse offers certainty without pausing to flatter the audience demand for an edited alternative.

phrases.translation: In fact, it is a confirmation of what came before, and an explanation of the Scripture.
phrases.explanation: Confirmation of what came before places the Quran in continuity with earlier revelation rather than as an isolated novelty. Explanation of the Scripture suggests detailed clarification of the central message carried across prophets. Continuity also creates a test, because the God who sent earlier guidance would not contradict His own unity and judgment. The verse therefore claims both inheritance and completion at once.

phrases.translation: It is, without a doubt, from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: Without doubt from the Lord of all worlds widens the source beyond a local tribe or sanctuary. A book for humanity needs an author whose lordship crosses the boundaries of its first audience. Doubt is denied after the arguments from creation, guidance, and history have accumulated. The line still functions as invitation, since certainty is meant to be recognised by reading rather than imposed by slogan.

phrases.translation: Or do they claim, “He made it up!”? Tell them ˹O Prophet˺,
phrases.explanation: He made it up is quoted so the charge can be tested rather than merely resented. Tell them places the answer in public, where poets, orators, priests, and tribal experts could hear it. A false accusation often survives by repetition in gatherings. The challenge interrupts that comfort by demanding work instead of talk, turning literary confidence into a task with witnesses.

phrases.translation: “Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can—
phrases.explanation: Produce one surah like it lowers the requested amount while raising the standard of resemblance. A single chapter should be easier than a whole book if human invention is the explanation. Seek help from whoever you can opens the workshop to every ally, human or claimed unseen. The generous conditions expose inability more clearly than a narrow contest would.

phrases.translation: other than Allah—if what you say is true!”
phrases.explanation: Other than Allah and if you are truthful bind the challenge to their accusation. They may use every created resource, because the question is whether created resources explain the Quran. Truthfulness becomes measurable through failure or success under stated terms. The verse does not ask them to admire eloquence in silence. It asks a culture proud of speech to meet speech on its own ground.

phrases.translation: In fact, they ˹hastily˺ rejected the Book without comprehending it and before the fulfilment of its warnings.
phrases.explanation: They rejected a Book whose knowledge they had not encompassed and whose interpretation or promised outcome had not yet reached them. Early commentators differed over whether interpretation means final explanation, promised punishment, or the reality of its reports. The shared fault is haste. Denial arrived before comprehension and before history finished speaking, which makes confidence look less like judgment than impatience.

phrases.translation: Similarly, those before them were in denial. See then what was the end of the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: Earlier deniers followed the same road, so the audience can study an ending already known. See what was the end directs eyes toward ruins, defeated tyrants, and vanished sanctuaries. Wrongdoers names people who placed themselves against proof and justice at once. The verse lets an unfinished present borrow clarity from a finished past, an education available to anyone willing to look.

phrases.translation: Some of them will ˹eventually˺ believe in it; others will not.
phrases.explanation: Some will believe later and some will not, a realistic division that frees the messenger from measuring truth by immediate totals. Delayed faith means present mockery does not always predict the final biography of a hearer. It also means persuasion cannot be forced into a single timetable. The verse keeps the door of preaching open while refusing to pretend every audience will move together.

phrases.translation: And your Lord knows best the corruptors
phrases.explanation: Your Lord knows best the corruptors places hidden quality above head counts. Corruption describes people who damage truth and society by organised denial, not every uncertain listener still searching. Knowing best allows the Prophet to continue without needing perfect classification of each face before him. Final sorting rests with God, while present duty remains clear speech and patience.

phrases.translation: If they deny you, then say, “My deeds are mine and your deeds are yours.
phrases.explanation: My deeds are mine and yours are yours creates a boundary when denial becomes settled. The sentence does not declare all choices equal. It assigns ownership, so the Prophet carries his obedience and opponents carry their rejection into judgment. Such separation can end fruitless argument without hatred in the moment, because the account has been clearly handed to each side.

phrases.translation: You are free of what I do and I am free of what you do!”
phrases.explanation: Free of what I do and free of what you do completes mutual dissociation from the other path. The Prophet refuses partnership in their denial, and they cannot claim his faith as social cover. Freedom here means innocence of the other record rather than freedom from consequence. It is a dignified withdrawal after delivery, useful where continued debate would only recycle refusal.

phrases.translation: Some of them listen to what you say, but can you make the deaf hear even though they do not understand
phrases.explanation: Listening without understanding is compared to deafness because sound reaches the ear while meaning does not reach the heart. The Prophet cannot manufacture comprehension inside a person who has closed the inner faculty. Deafness in the image is moral and intellectual rather than a comment on people with hearing loss. The verse consoles a teacher whose clear speech still meets a wall built by refusal.

phrases.translation: And some of them look at you, but can you guide the blind even though they cannot see
phrases.explanation: Looking without seeing repeats the same problem through the eyes. A person may observe the Prophet character, the community change, and signs in creation while interpreting every sight through a prior refusal. Blindness names the failure to let sight become guidance. Again the limit belongs to the messenger role, since he can present the road clearly but cannot walk it inside another person skin.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah does not wrong people in the least, but it is people who wrong themselves
phrases.explanation: Allah wrongs no one in the least, a principle that guards every hard statement about sealed refusal in the chapter. People wrong themselves by closing hearing, sight, and reflection until guidance sounds like noise. Self wronging explains how judgment can be severe without becoming arbitrary. The verse gives the reader a scale for all the destroyed nations, storms, and futures described around it.

phrases.translation: On the Day He will gather them, it will be as if they had not stayed ˹in the world˺ except for an hour of a day,
phrases.explanation: On the gathering Day, a whole earthly life shrinks to an hour of a day. Resurrection changes the scale by which duration is felt, so decades of work, conflict, and building resemble a morning visit. The image does not deny that life felt long while lived. It predicts how small it will look once an unending horizon opens in front of the soul.

phrases.translation: ˹as though they were only˺ getting to know one another.
phrases.explanation: Getting to know one another adds social thinness to the shortened time. Generations who filled the earth will seem like travellers who exchanged names at a station before moving on. Fame, feud, wealth, and ancestry lose their apparent bulk in that first sight. The verse works quietly against worldly pride, because even a celebrated biography can become an hour when measured from eternity.

phrases.translation: Lost indeed will be those who denied the meeting with Allah, and were not ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: Lost indeed names those who denied the meeting and were not guided. Their loss is sharper because the brief hour was spent preparing for the wrong scale. Guidance would have taught them to invest the little time in faith and good deeds before the gathering exposed its size. The verse therefore turns a future impression into present advice about clocks and priorities.

phrases.translation: Whether We show you ˹O Prophet˺ some of what We threaten them with,
phrases.explanation: Whether the Prophet lives to see part of the threatened outcome or dies before it, his duty does not change. History may unveil judgment in stages through defeat, exposure, or death, yet no stage needs his presence to remain valid. The sentence frees a messenger from demanding a personal front seat at vindication. Delivery is complete even when consequences ripen later.

phrases.translation: or cause you to die ˹before that˺, to Us is their return and Allah is a Witness over what they do
phrases.explanation: Their return is to Allah and He witnesses what they do, which closes every gap left by an unfinished lifetime. Witness means deeds are observed now, not reconstructed from rumour at the end. People who escape a prophet lifetime do not escape the record formed within it. The verse gives patience a firm base, because delay is carried inside knowledge rather than absence.

phrases.translation: And for every community there is a messenger. After their messenger has come,
phrases.explanation: Every community has a messenger makes the present audience part of a universal pattern rather than an exception. Guidance is sent in human form across history, with languages and settings fitted to peoples. After the messenger comes, responsibility changes because the road has been named from inside their world. The verse dignifies earlier nations while removing any claim that God judged without sending.

phrases.translation: judgment is passed on them in all fairness, and they are not wronged
phrases.explanation: Judgment in fairness follows the messenger arrival, whether the settling occurs in history, at resurrection, or across both in early readings. They are not wronged repeats the moral guarantee that evidence and capacity matter. A community may receive years of preaching before its end. Fairness therefore includes time and clarity, not only an exact final sentence after refusal hardens.

phrases.translation: They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass if what you say is true?”
phrases.explanation: When will this threat be fulfilled turns a warning into a timetable challenge. The question can sound brave, yet it often assumes that anything not scheduled publicly is unreal. If what you say is true places the burden on timing rather than on the evidence already offered. The verse captures a style of denial that uses calendars to avoid conscience, as though a later date would weaken a certain appointment.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I have no power to benefit or protect myself, except by the Will of Allah.”
phrases.explanation: The Prophet owns no independent power to harm or benefit even himself except as Allah wills. That confession answers demands for signs and dates by locating control in the sender rather than the messenger. A man who cannot schedule his own protection cannot be treated as the manager of judgment. His limitation strengthens his credibility, because an inventor seeking status would be tempted to promise control.

phrases.translation: For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they cannot delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it
phrases.explanation: Each community has an appointed term that cannot be delayed or advanced by a moment when it arrives. The image is of an exact boundary hidden inside what feels like open time. Nations, like individuals, live within a span that argument cannot stretch. This certainty makes postponement less comforting, because every ordinary day is moving inside a term already written.

phrases.translation: Tell them ˹O Prophet˺, “Imagine if His torment were to overcome you by night or day—
phrases.explanation: Imagine punishment arriving by night or day removes the imagined safety of choosing a convenient hour. Night finds people asleep and unprepared, while day finds them busy and distracted by work. Either way the event does not consult their diary. The question is designed to make a threatened future enter the senses, because abstract warnings often fail until a scene gives them walls and darkness.

phrases.translation: do the wicked realize what they are ˹really˺ asking Him to hasten
phrases.explanation: What part of it would the guilty hasten asks them to inspect their own request. Hurry makes sense for rain, rescue, or payment, not for torment whose arrival ends bargaining. Mocking speed becomes irrational once the object is pictured accurately. The verse does not yet answer when. It asks why anyone who understood what might come would treat delay as evidence against it.

phrases.translation: Will you believe in it only after it has overtaken you?
phrases.explanation: Belief after punishment overtakes a person is pictured as recognition without benefit. Seeing the flood, army, or final terror removes doubt at exactly the moment when choice has narrowed. Earlier verses praised faith that acts while the road remains open. This question therefore protects the value of present belief, because certainty purchased by disaster cannot perform the deeds that earlier time made possible.

phrases.translation: Now? But you always wanted to hasten it!”
phrases.explanation: Now is repeated with bitter surprise, answering their former eagerness to hasten the event. The word makes the delay they mocked appear as mercy they spent carelessly. A deadline can look unreal from far away and absolute from close range without the deadline changing at all. The verse leaves the sound of now in the ear as a warning for readers still living before it.

phrases.translation: Then the wrongdoers will be told, “Taste the torment of eternity!
phrases.explanation: Taste the punishment of eternity speaks to wrongdoers after recognition has arrived too late. Taste makes the consequence immediate and personal rather than a theory about history. Eternity removes the hope that endurance will eventually turn a corner into release. The opening tone is judicial rather than taunting, because the next clause will tie the experience exactly to deeds.

phrases.translation: Are you not rewarded except for what you used to commit?”
phrases.explanation: Are you rewarded except for what you earned asks whether any foreign element has been added to the account. The answer expected is no, since the life of denial, cruelty, and mockery has matured into its result. Reward is again fitting return rather than gift. This symmetry matters because people who once called warnings unfair are shown a ledger written by their own repeated choices.

phrases.translation: They ask you ˹O Prophet˺, “Is this true?” Say, “Yes, by my Lord!
phrases.explanation: Is it true receives an oath by my Lord rather than another timetable. The Prophet is commanded to swear because the question concerns reality itself, not a date he controls. Repetition in most certainly gives the answer a settled weight after many verses of argument. An oath also places his own credibility under God, continuing the pattern of a messenger who refuses independent authority.

phrases.translation: Most certainly it is true! And you will have no escape.”
phrases.explanation: No escape closes the imagined exits of wealth, tribe, argument, and delay. The Arabic sense includes being unable to frustrate Allah or slip outside His reach. People can evade a human court by distance or influence, yet return remains built into existence. The sentence is short because all the earlier parables have already shown fields cut down and ships surrounded.

phrases.translation: If every wrongdoer were to possess everything in the world, they would surely ransom themselves with it.
phrases.explanation: If a wrongdoer owned everything on earth, the whole sum would be offered as ransom at the sight of punishment. Wealth changes value when pain becomes permanent and near. Things once protected from charity and justice would be surrendered in a moment. The hypothetical exposes earthly accumulation as a poor ultimate security, since the owner finally prices the soul above the entire estate.

phrases.translation: They will hide ˹their˺ remorse when they see the torment.
phrases.explanation: They will conceal remorse when they see punishment, whether hiding it from followers, from one another, or within a heart too proud to display collapse. Early commentators discussed the scene, including leaders concealing regret before those they misled. Hidden sorrow adds isolation to pain. Even at the end, image management may survive for a moment, although it can no longer change the account.

phrases.translation: And they will be judged in all fairness, and none will be wronged
phrases.explanation: Judged in fairness and not wronged returns after the ransom image to prevent despair from misreading the court. No bribe succeeds, yet no extra charge is invented either. Fairness is good news for the oppressed and a precise warning for oppressors. The verse ends by assuring readers that final judgment is terrifying because it is exact, not because it is careless.

phrases.translation: Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: Whatever is in heavens and earth belongs to Allah, which answers the ransom wish at its root. A person cannot buy release from the Owner using property already held under His ownership. Earthly title deeds operate between people for a lifetime, then lose force at return. The statement also widens the mind from local wealth to a kingdom no human fortune can approach.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true, but most of them do not know
phrases.explanation: The promise is true although most do not know may mean many do not know its reality, timing, or the value of what is promised. Ignorance here follows heedlessness rather than lack of announcements, since signs and messengers have filled the passage. Majority unawareness does not dilute truth. The verse teaches the Prophet audience to measure certainty by the speaker, not by counting who presently feels convinced.

phrases.translation: He ˹is the One Who˺ gives life and causes death, and to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation: Giving life and causing death gathers the two boundaries that no partner or fortune can move. Return to Him completes the arc, so the same power that starts and ends earthly life also receives its account. The one verse stands like a summary after arguments about ransom and promise. It gives resurrection a personal direction, because people are not merely reappearing. They are coming back to Someone.

phrases.translation: O humanity! Indeed, there has come to you a warning from your Lord,
phrases.explanation: O humanity widens the address after arguments with a particular audience, announcing an admonition from their Lord. A warning or exhortation speaks to conduct before it heals feeling, since people need direction as well as comfort. From your Lord stresses care in the source. The Quran presents itself here as medicine delivered by the One who made the heart rather than advice gathered from competing customs.

phrases.translation: a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers
phrases.explanation: A cure for what is in the chests names doubt, hypocrisy, resentment, ignorance, and divided loyalty as diseases needing treatment. Guidance then gives the road after diagnosis, while mercy for believers describes the experienced result of accepting both. The sequence matters because information alone may not heal a resentful heart. Revelation is pictured as working from the inside outward, until belief becomes health rather than merely correct vocabulary.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “In Allah’s grace and mercy let them rejoice.
phrases.explanation: In the bounty and mercy of Allah let them rejoice redirects celebration toward revelation itself. Grace may include Islam and the Quran in early explanation, gifts received rather than manufactured by effort. Joy is not cancelled by religion in this verse. It is educated, so the heart learns to throw its festival around guidance instead of every temporary increase in possessions.

phrases.translation: That is far better than whatever ˹wealth˺ they amass.”
phrases.explanation: Better than what they amass compares a healing Book with stored wealth on the scale of final benefit. Money can be counted, guarded, and displayed, yet it cannot cure the chest or ransom the soul. The verse does not require contempt for lawful provision. It forbids accumulation from taking first place in joy, because the thing that saves a life should be loved more than things.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹the pagans, O Prophet˺, “Have you seen that which Allah has sent down for you as a provision,
phrases.explanation: Have you seen the provision turns food and livestock into a test of religious authority. Allah sends provision down through rain, earth, animals, and human labour, yet people carve it into sacred categories of their own. The question starts with sight because the evidence grazes and grows in front of them. A created gift has been fenced by rules whose source now needs examination.

phrases.translation: of which you have made some lawful and some unlawful?”
phrases.explanation: Making some lawful and some unlawful refers to pre Islamic customs that reserved certain animals or crops through vows and superstitions. Such rules could burden the poor and enrich custodians while sounding devout. Lawful and unlawful are powerful words because they bind conscience in Allah name. The verse asks whether a human tradition has borrowed divine authority without permission.

phrases.translation: Say, “Has Allah given you authorization, or are you fabricating lies against Allah?”
phrases.explanation: Has Allah authorised you or are you fabricating places every religious rule before two possible sources. There is no third shelter called harmless custom once a practice is imposed as God law. Fabrication does not require inventing a whole scripture. It can happen in a food rule, a festival ban, or a priestly fee that quietly claims heaven approval without evidence.

phrases.translation: What do those who fabricate lies against Allah expect on Judgment Day?
phrases.explanation: What do fabricators think of Judgment Day asks them to imagine explaining invented rules before the Lawgiver. Human beings may obey a false prohibition for generations, creating guilt and hardship in Allah name. The thought of that Day exposes the seriousness behind what looks like a minor dietary custom. A lie about God has a future audience with God built into it.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most of them are ungrateful
phrases.explanation: Bounty toward humanity and widespread ingratitude close the discussion with a wider pattern. Allah gives provision, time, revelation, and repeated chances, while many respond by editing His gifts or inventing burdens. Ingratitude can therefore take a religious costume rather than open denial. The verse turns criticism of pagans into a mirror for any community tempted to add rules while neglecting thanks.

phrases.translation: There is no activity you may be engaged in ˹O Prophet˺ or portion of the Quran you may be reciting,
phrases.explanation: No state of the Prophet and no portion of Quran he recites stands outside divine witness. The address begins with the most honoured person in the audience so observation cannot be imagined as suspicion directed only at opponents. Work, worship, and public recitation all happen before Allah. This awareness steadies a messenger whose opponents try to make private plots feel larger than the open eye of heaven.

phrases.translation: nor any deed you ˹all˺ may be doing except that We are a Witness over you while doing it.
phrases.explanation: Nor any deed you all do widens the witness from Prophet to every actor in the story. While you are engaged in it stresses the present tense, since Allah does not learn about events after reports arrive. Hidden planning, public charity, recitation, and mockery are seen at the moment of intention and performance. The verse turns surveillance language into moral presence, calling each side to act as already observed.

phrases.translation: Not ˹even˺ an atom’s weight is hidden from your Lord on earth or in heaven;
phrases.explanation: An atom weight presents the smallest imagined unit as still fully known on earth or in heaven. The image is not mainly about physical particles as later science uses the term. It uses tiny weight to defeat the hope that some deed is too small, distant, or buried to matter. Conscience often dismisses minor words, yet the record has no minimum size below which responsibility disappears.

phrases.translation: nor anything smaller or larger than that, but is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record
phrases.explanation: Smaller or larger than that in a clear Record completes the scale. Clarity suggests the record makes deeds plain when the time comes rather than storing them in confusion. The verse bridges the inner and outer worlds, because a God aware of atoms cannot miss motives. Comfort follows for hidden good as surely as warning follows for hidden plotting, and that double edge leads directly to the friends of Allah.

phrases.translation: There will certainly be no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation: Close servants of Allah, often called His friends or allies, are promised freedom from fear and grief. Fear usually looks toward future harm while grief looks back at loss, so the promise covers both directions of human pain. Nearness to Allah does not mean a life without hardship in this world. It means hardship cannot decide the final emotional state of those held by such a guardian.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who are faithful and are mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: Those who believe and remain mindful defines closeness without mystery or inherited title. Faith supplies the relationship, while mindfulness protects it through daily choices about speech, money, appetite, and power. The short definition democratises a high station that people may reserve for famous saints. A hidden believer guarding conduct in ordinary work stands inside the description as surely as a public figure of devotion.

phrases.translation: For them is good news in this worldly life and the Hereafter.
phrases.explanation: Good news in this life and the Hereafter spreads their assurance across both worlds. Early commentators mentioned true dreams, love placed in people hearts, praise, and calm at death among the worldly glad tidings, while Paradise remains the complete form. The phrase allows several gifts without reducing the promise to one sign. A believer may taste nearness now without mistaking the taste for the final home.

phrases.translation: There is no change in the promise of Allah. That is ˹truly˺ the ultimate triumph
phrases.explanation: No change in the words of Allah makes the promise stable across moods, regimes, and public opinion. Ultimate triumph here is not merely escaping punishment. It is living and dying inside a guardianship that cannot be voted away by enemies. In a chapter where crowds mock and storms frighten, unchanging words give the heart a fixed point. The greatest success is a relationship secured by God Himself.

phrases.translation: Do not let their words grieve you ˹O Prophet˺. Surely all honour and power belongs to Allah. He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: Do not let their speech grieve you speaks to a Prophet who hears insults, threats, and confident falsehood as part of delivery. Honour belongs entirely to Allah, so human voices cannot remove dignity God has assigned. All Hearing and All Knowing assure him that words are neither unheard nor misunderstood in heaven. The verse treats grief honestly while refusing to let an audience become the measure of worth.

phrases.translation: Certainly to Allah ˹alone˺ belong all those in the heavens and all those on the earth.
phrases.explanation: All in heavens and earth belong to Allah alone, including angels, humans, animals, and every being some group might promote into partnership. Ownership answers worship more deeply than power alone, because owned servants cannot share the throne of their Owner. The verse also comforts believers surrounded by crowds, since opponents themselves live inside the kingdom of the Lord they resist.

phrases.translation: And what do those who associate others with Allah really follow?
phrases.explanation: What do those who call on partners really follow asks for the substance beneath ritual confidence. Names, statues, ancestors, and unseen claims may fill a sanctuary while the path rests on no revealed proof. Reality language strips away ceremony to inspect foundation. A crowded religious life can still be following an idea nobody received from Allah, and numbers do not turn that idea into a road.

phrases.translation: They follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie
phrases.explanation: Assumption and lying form the answer, with lying here carrying the sense of guessing and speaking without knowledge as much as deliberate deceit in every case. A person may inherit the guess sincerely and still be following a falsehood. The verse challenges method rather than merely accusing character. Claims about God need a source that can survive examination when custom stops applauding.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who has made the night for you to rest in and the day bright.
phrases.explanation: Night made for rest and day made bright reverse the usual human wish to treat darkness as interruption. Sleep restores bodies, hides vulnerability, cools labour, and allows families and worship to gather in another mode. Bright day gives sight for work and travel. Together they form a daily mercy so regular that gratitude usually sleeps inside it, exactly while the gift is being received.

phrases.translation: Surely in this are signs for people who listen
phrases.explanation: Signs for people who listen closes the verse with hearing rather than seeing, although the evidence is visible. Listening means receiving the lesson carried by a cycle, not only registering noise. A person can watch ten thousand sunsets and remain untaught, while another hears one nightfall as a sermon on dependence. The verse therefore makes receptivity the organ by which the sky speaks.

phrases.translation: They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient.
phrases.explanation: Allah has taken a son or offspring is answered first with glory be to Him and then Self Sufficient. A child in human life answers need, continuity, support, and likeness, none of which can be imagined as a deficiency in God within Quranic teaching. The claim is treated theologically rather than as a comment on individual worth. Divine richness means perfect freedom from need.

phrases.translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.
phrases.explanation: All in heavens and earth belongs to Him removes any region where an alleged offspring could stand as an independent partner. A son in their claim would still be created and owned if located anywhere in existence, which contradicts divine sonship as equality. Ownership therefore does argumentative work. Everything named by worshippers returns quickly to servant status once the whole map is remembered.

phrases.translation: You have no proof of this! Do you say about Allah what you do not know
phrases.explanation: You have no authority or proof for this demands evidence for a statement about Allah inner reality. Do you say what you do not know turns loose sacred talk into a serious offence, especially when it is repeated by scripture communities or pagan custom. Reverent silence is safer than inherited certainty without revelation. The verse defends both unity and intellectual honesty at the same time.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will never succeed.”
phrases.explanation: Fabricators against Allah will never succeed repeats the verdict from verse seventeen after the sonship claim. Success may appear as followers, institutions, wealth, or books built around an invented statement, yet final failure remains written into the enterprise. A lie about the highest reality cannot become ultimate prosperity simply by surviving for centuries. The verse asks readers to judge movements at their end rather than by their architecture.

phrases.translation: ˹It is only˺ a brief enjoyment in this world, then to Us is their return,
phrases.explanation: Brief enjoyment in this world permits a lie to flourish socially without changing its final value. Food, status, sexual freedom, income, and applause may all be gathered around a false claim for a season. Then to Us is their return limits the season with the chapter recurring destination. A crowded present can still be a short lease, and time spent inside it does not become ownership of eternity.
