phrases.translation: then We will make them taste the severe punishment for their disbelief
phrases.explanation: Severe punishment tasted for disbelief completes the exchange. Taste again makes judgment experiential rather than theoretical, while the reason is tied to persistent rejection instead of a mistake made in ignorance. Worldly enjoyment was also tasted, so the two experiences stand in deliberate contrast. The verse compresses a biography into sample and settlement, asking which flavour a person is preparing to know last.

phrases.translation: Relate to them ˹O Prophet˺ the story of Noah when he said to his people, “O my People!
phrases.explanation: The story of Noah is introduced as news worth relating because a long rejected ministry speaks directly to the Prophet situation. O my people keeps kinship and compassion inside a confrontation, since Noah addresses opponents as his own rather than strangers. Ancient history becomes present instruction without erasing the distance in time. The reader is asked to hear a familiar prophetic pattern from its earliest large example.

phrases.translation: If my presence and my reminders to you of Allah’s signs are unbearable to you,
phrases.explanation: If my standing and reminders feel heavy to you names the real irritation, namely his continued presence with signs. A preacher can become unbearable simply by refusing to disappear, because each reminder reopens a decision people wanted closed. Noah does not soften the message to relieve the weight. He first acknowledges their feeling honestly, which makes his next act of trust more striking.

phrases.translation: then ˹know that˺ I have put my trust in Allah.
phrases.explanation: On Allah I have relied brings his security out of clan protection and public approval. Trust here follows centuries of rejection in the broader story, so it is not the optimism of a beginner. He gives opponents no power to set the limit of his obedience by threatening isolation. A messenger whose support is vertical can remain truthful when horizontal support has almost vanished.

phrases.translation: So devise a plot along with your associate-gods—and you do not have to be secretive about your plot—
phrases.explanation: Decide your affair openly with your partners challenges them to stop hiding behind delay and whispered pressure. Let your plan cause you no distress or concealment suggests that every resource and alleged god should be gathered without embarrassment. The openness exposes the partnership test once more. If their gods can help, a public plan is the moment to prove it rather than another season of insinuation.

phrases.translation: then carry it out against me without delay
phrases.explanation: Then carry it out against me without delay completes a speech of remarkable calm. Noah is not seeking harm for its own sake. He is withdrawing the leverage of suspense from people who govern through threat. Trust becomes visible when a person refuses to bargain away a message for safety. The verse gives later believers a grammar for courage that does not depend on matching enemy numbers.

phrases.translation: And if you turn away, ˹remember˺ I have never demanded a reward from you ˹for delivering the message˺.
phrases.explanation: No wage demanded removes a common suspicion from preaching. If the audience turns away, Noah loses no salary, market, or patronage because none was being collected. Free delivery protects the message from sounding like a product adjusted for buyers. It also exposes rejection as a response to the content rather than anger at a fee, which is why messengers repeat the point across stories.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from Allah. And I have been commanded to be one of those who submit ˹to Allah˺.”
phrases.explanation: My reward is only with Allah and I am commanded to submit joins payment and posture. Noah belongs to the community he calls into being, under the same Lord and the same obedience. Submission here translates the identity later named Muslim in its broad sense of one who surrenders to God. He does not stand outside the demand as a contractor. His wage and his worship point in one direction.

phrases.translation: But they still rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the Ark and made them successors,
phrases.explanation: They still denied him and Allah saved Noah with those in the Ark, making survivors successors on the earth. A tiny believing company becomes the seed of the next human order after judgment. Successors echoes verse fourteen, because receiving the land after ruin carries responsibility rather than pride. The Ark is both rescue and examination paper handed to a renewed generation.

phrases.translation: and drowned those who rejected Our signs.
phrases.explanation: Drowning those who denied the signs gives water the final word over a people who treated warning as background noise. Across this chapter the sea rescued sailors who called sincerely and here it removes persistent deniers, so nature follows command rather than a fixed mood. Denial of signs, not simply being caught in weather, explains the end. The precision matters because the flood is judgment, not accident.

phrases.translation: See then what was the end of those who had been warned
phrases.explanation: See the end of those who were warned turns narrative into inspection. Warning had stretched across a long ministry, removing the excuse that judgment came without a voice. The reader is not asked merely to admire Noah patience. The reader must study the destination of warned refusal and decide whether present delay is truly safer than repentance. History ends as a signpost rather than entertainment.

phrases.translation: Then after him We sent ˹other˺ messengers to their ˹own˺ people and they came to them with clear proofs.
phrases.explanation: After Noah, messengers kept coming to their own peoples with clear proofs, showing that rejection is not one isolated ancient temperament. Each setting received a known voice, local language, and evidence suited to its claims. Repetition builds a sociology of denial across centuries. The present audience is therefore not being compared with monsters from fable but with ordinary communities protecting familiar arrangements.

phrases.translation: But they would not believe in what they had rejected before.
phrases.explanation: They would not believe in what they had denied before describes the hardening created by an earlier no. First rejection can become identity, after which every new proof is filtered to protect the original decision. Time does not automatically soften a person. It can practise the heart in refusal until openness feels like betrayal of ancestors, friends, or the self built around resistance.

phrases.translation: This is how We seal the hearts of the transgressors
phrases.explanation: Sealing hearts of transgressors presents the final state of that practised refusal. A seal closes a container against new contents, an image suited to evidence repeated without entry. In the Quran moral pattern, sealing follows crossing limits rather than preceding innocent choice. The verse warns readers early, because today casual dismissal may be the first layer of a closure they will later call inability.

phrases.translation: Then after these ˹messengers˺ We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs.
phrases.explanation: Moses and Aaron sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs moves the pattern from tribal denial to imperial power. Two brothers carry signs to a court that controls labour, armies, priests, and the story public life tells about itself. Naming chiefs matters because tyranny rarely operates through one man alone. A whole circle benefits from the arrangement and therefore helps protect it against unwelcome truth.

phrases.translation: But they behaved arrogantly and were a wicked people
phrases.explanation: They were arrogant and criminal identifies the court response before detailed signs are listed. Arrogance is not lack of information but refusal to kneel when information threatens rank. Criminal or guilty joins inner posture with public oppression, especially the enslavement surrounding the mission. The verse frames the coming contest as humility before God against a system invested in staying unanswerable.

phrases.translation: When the truth came to them from Us, they said, “This is certainly pure magic!”
phrases.explanation: Pure magic is the court verdict on truth when it arrives with signs. The label allows Pharaoh circle to preserve expertise, since a magician can be answered by hiring better magicians rather than by obeying God. Earlier the Prophet heard the same word in Mecca. Skilled regimes and status groups often prefer a category they manage to a claim that would judge the managers.

phrases.translation: Moses responded, “Is this what you say about the truth when it has come to you?
phrases.explanation: Moses repeats their charge as a question, forcing the court to hear what it has called the truth after its arrival. Repetition exposes the decision hidden inside the label. They did not test the signs first and classify them second. The classification arrived as protection for the throne. A question can therefore be a mirror, especially when powerful people prefer naming to thinking.

phrases.translation: Is this magic? Magicians will never succeed.”
phrases.explanation: Is this magic and magicians will never succeed separates prophetic signs from professional illusion by outcome and purpose. Magic in the story works on eyes and public fear, while truth carries a moral claim that liberates slaves and judges tyranny. Success again means final success before Allah rather than applause in a contest. The sentence predicts the court experts will lose on their chosen ground.

phrases.translation: They argued, “Have you come to turn us away from the faith of our forefathers so that the two of you may become supreme in the land? We will never believe in you!”
phrases.explanation: The accusation becomes political, namely that Moses and Aaron want to replace ancestral religion and seize greatness in the land. Ancestors supply emotional authority, while suspicion of ambition gives the court a motive to discuss instead of evidence. We will never believe is declared before the contest has even been staged. The verse shows denial protecting both identity and an economy built around Pharaoh order.

phrases.translation: Pharaoh demanded, “Bring me every skilled magician.”
phrases.explanation: Bring every skilled magician turns an empire resources toward stage management. Skilled or knowing suggests the best professionals available, gathered so the palace can win by spectacle and numbers. Pharaoh does not ask priests to pray for truth. He commissions a performance. The short command reveals how power often responds to a moral challenge by looking for technicians who can restore the old picture.

phrases.translation: When the magicians came, Moses said to them, “Cast whatever you wish to cast!”
phrases.explanation: Moses tells the assembled magicians to throw first, a calm courtesy that also displays confidence. Their ropes and staffs will be allowed to create the strongest possible impression before his sign answers. No bargaining over order suggests the outcome does not depend on surprise. In a court built on intimidation, letting opponents begin becomes a form of dignity, because truth does not need to rush an illusion off stage.

phrases.translation: When they did, Moses said, “What you have produced is mere magic,
phrases.explanation: What they produced is named magic only after they have acted, reversing the court earlier use of the label. Their craft makes objects appear alive and fills watchers with fear in the wider account. Moses identifies the category without denying the skill involved. The distinction matters because an impressive effect can be real as performance while false as a claim about ultimate power.

phrases.translation: Allah will surely make it useless, for Allah certainly does not set right the work of the corruptors
phrases.explanation: Allah will make their work void and does not repair the work of corruptors gives the coming defeat a moral rule. Techniques used to defend oppression may shine for an hour and still lack divine support. Setting right suggests success, stability, and approval, none of which corruption can rent from God. Before the staff moves, Moses announces the principle by which spectators should read the result.

phrases.translation: And Allah establishes the truth by His Words—even to the dismay of the wicked.”
phrases.explanation: Allah confirms truth by His words even when the guilty dislike every step of its arrival. Words can include commands, promises, and the decreed outcomes that make revelation visible in history. Dislike does not function as a veto in this universe. The closing line lifts the contest from entertainment into judgment, because the court wanted applause while heaven was establishing a verdict.

phrases.translation: But no one believed in Moses except a few youths of his people, while fearing that Pharaoh and their own chiefs might persecute them.
phrases.explanation: Only a small group from Moses people believed at first, often explained as youths or a limited number from the Children of Israel, and they did so under fear of persecution. Faith under surveillance grows quietly because public allegiance can cost work, safety, and family standing. Their smallness should not be read as weakness of truth. It measures the pressure created by a state skilled at punishing hope.

phrases.translation: And certainly Pharaoh was a tyrant in the land, and he was truly a transgressor
phrases.explanation: Pharaoh was exalted in the land and among the transgressors, a social fact behind their fear. Exalted catches public posture, forced labour, court ritual, and military reach in one word. Transgressor names the moral side of the same height. The verse validates why young believers trembled while still honouring their decision, because courage is not the absence of fear but faith acting inside it.

phrases.translation: Moses said, “O my people! If you do believe in Allah and submit ˹to His Will˺, then put your trust in Him.”
phrases.explanation: Moses calls his people to connect belief, submission, and trust in one practical chain. If they truly trust Allah, Pharaoh threats cannot remain the organising centre of life. Submission gives trust a direction, since reliance without obedience can become wishful thinking. The short sermon is addressed to frightened people rather than comfortable theorists, and it gives fear a place to go besides surrender to the tyrant.

phrases.translation: They replied, “In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Do not subject us to the persecution of the oppressive people
phrases.explanation: Their reply begins with trust before asking not to be made a trial for oppressive people. Early explanations include not letting the tyrants overpower them and then claim that power proves truth, and not letting suffering become a means by which oppressors are emboldened. The prayer is social as well as personal. They ask that their weakness not be used as propaganda for injustice.

phrases.translation: and deliver us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.”
phrases.explanation: Deliverance by mercy from the disbelieving people completes the prayer with the only rescue that can end the whole condition. They do not merely ask for private comfort under slavery. They ask to be brought out of the power of a people defined by rejection and oppression. Mercy frames liberation as gift rather than wages, an important note for a frightened minority whose resources could never purchase a nation.

phrases.translation: We revealed to Moses and his brother, “Appoint houses for your people in Egypt.
phrases.explanation: Houses in Egypt are appointed for the people before any exodus route opens. God instructs Moses and Aaron to organise domestic space under oppression, giving scattered families recognisable homes within the land of their labour. Preparation begins where they already live. Liberation movements in the verse include address, gathering, and the slow formation of a people who can move as more than individual sufferers.

phrases.translation: Turn these houses into places of worship, establish prayer, and give good news to the believers!”
phrases.explanation: Making houses places of worship or facing in prayer, as early commentators explored both aspects, turns the home into a sanctuary when public worship is dangerous. Establish prayer keeps rhythm under surveillance, while good news to believers prevents secrecy from shrinking hope. The verse shows that resistance may begin with prayer mats in ordinary rooms. Before the sea opens, time itself is reclaimed from Pharaoh.

phrases.translation: Moses prayed, “Our Lord! You have granted Pharaoh and his chiefs luxuries and riches in this worldly life,
phrases.explanation: Moses prayer begins by acknowledging that Pharaoh splendour and wealth came under divine permission in worldly life. Palaces, ornaments, treasuries, and court display were not outside the knowledge of God while they intimidated slaves. Naming the source keeps the prayer from sounding like surprise at a rival kingdom. It asks the true Owner to judge what temporary ownership has produced.

phrases.translation: ˹which they abused˺ to lead people astray from Your Way!
phrases.explanation: Their wealth has been used to lead people from the path, because spectacle makes tyranny look blessed and gives experts reasons to serve it. Riches in the wrong hands purchase magicians, soldiers, informers, and silence. Moses complaint is not envy of luxury. It concerns the moral work luxury performs when a population reads gold as proof that heaven approves the throne.

phrases.translation: Our Lord, destroy their riches and harden their hearts so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.”
phrases.explanation: Destroy their riches and harden their hearts is a severe prayer after long signs and refusal, asking that wealth lose its power and that persistent rebellion reach its chosen closure until punishment is seen. It should not be detached into a casual model for cursing opponents. In the story it belongs to a prophet at the end of an imperial confrontation after evidence has been exhausted.

phrases.translation: Allah responded ˹to Moses and Aaron˺, “Your prayer is answered!
phrases.explanation: Your prayer is answered is spoken in a form that includes Aaron, because he joined Moses in the mission and the supplication circuit around it. An answered prayer may still unfold through plagues, pursuit, and sea rather than instant disappearance of the court. Certainty about the end can coexist with a road that remains frightening. The verse gives assurance before visibility, which is where steadfastness is most needed.

phrases.translation: So be steadfast and do not follow the way of those who do not know.”
phrases.explanation: Remain steadfast and do not follow the way of those who do not know instructs winners before victory has appeared. Ignorance could tempt them toward panic, imitation of Pharaoh methods, or doubt when events slow down. Straightness is therefore a discipline after good news, not only during bad news. The two brothers must keep walking the assigned road while the answered prayer catches up in history.

phrases.translation: We brought the Children of Israel across the sea. Then Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them unjustly and oppressively.
phrases.explanation: The Children of Israel cross the sea under divine action, then Pharaoh pursues in hatred and aggression. The same water becomes road and wall depending on the command. Pursuit after slaves have already departed shows that Pharaoh cannot accept a world in which his ownership has ended. Empire follows its former property into the sea because pride treats even the sea floor as court territory.

phrases.translation: But as Pharaoh was drowning, he cried out, “I believe that there is no god except that in whom the Children of Israel believe,
phrases.explanation: Drowning produces the confession Pharaoh refused through signs, plagues, and arguments. He names the God of the Children of Israel because the slaves he despised have become the safest theological address available. Belief spoken when the water closes may be factually accurate while arriving outside the time of testing. The scene returns to verse fifty one, where belief after being overtaken was questioned.

phrases.translation: and I am ˹now˺ one of those who submit.”
phrases.explanation: I am among those who submit tries to join the departing community at the last breath. Submission as an identity had been available through repentance, release of slaves, and humility before signs. At this point it functions as a rescue request from consequences rather than a changed life. The tragedy is precise, because the words are right while the biography speaking them has run out of future.

phrases.translation: ˹He was told,˺ “Now ˹you believe˺? But you always disobeyed and were one of the corruptors
phrases.explanation: Now, after a lifetime of disobedience and corruption, is the divine reply to the drowning confession. The question does not mock repentance in ordinary life, where return remains open before death is witnessed. It addresses a tyrant whose confession begins only when punishment is physically upon him. The repeated now from earlier in the chapter now lands on the most powerful man in the story.

phrases.translation: Today We will preserve your corpse so that you may become an example for those who come after you.
phrases.explanation: Today We save your body or preserve your corpse makes Pharaoh remains a sign for later generations. Commentators discussed the body being cast up so followers could know he had truly died, while the basic lesson remains clear. The ruler who claimed exaltation becomes evidence that can be looked at. Power ends in a body that cannot command even its own burial story.

phrases.translation: And surely most people are heedless of Our examples!”
phrases.explanation: Most people are heedless of Our signs ends the episode by turning from the corpse to its audience. A preserved warning still requires eyes willing to learn from a drowned empire. Museums, ruins, and stories can all be consumed as curiosity without repentance. Heedlessness links Pharaoh followers to every later reader who studies tyranny as spectacle while ignoring the same appetite in a smaller throne.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We settled the Children of Israel in a blessed land, and granted them good, lawful provisions.
phrases.explanation: A blessed settlement and good provisions answer generations of slavery with land, security, and lawful sustenance. The Children of Israel receive what Pharaoh order denied them, including a place where worship and ordinary life can be organised. Grace after rescue matters because liberation is incomplete if a people survive the sea only to starve on the shore. Settlement turns escape into the beginning of responsibility.

phrases.translation: They did not differ until knowledge came to them. Surely your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their differences
phrases.explanation: They did not differ until knowledge came to them is a sobering diagnosis of later division. Ignorance alone does not explain every dispute, since people can split after revelation through rivalry, ambition, and selective reading. Judgment on the Day will settle matters that history leaves contested. The verse warns the new audience that receiving knowledge creates a fresh test about how knowledge will be carried.

phrases.translation: If you ˹O Prophet˺ are in doubt about ˹these stories˺ that We have revealed to you,
phrases.explanation: If you are in doubt addresses the Prophet in a conditional form that early commentators often read as instruction for hearers or as a rhetorical way to confirm the report, not as an accusation that he doubted. The stories of Moses and earlier peoples arrived to a man who had not been trained in their scriptures. That setting makes confirmation from older sources part of the public argument.

phrases.translation: then ask those who read the Scripture before you.
phrases.explanation: Ask those who read the Scripture before you points to learned Jews and Christians who could recognise the broad prophetic history. Consultation here does not make them judges over revelation. It uses their existing records as a witness that the Quran story belongs to a known sequence. A new messenger can stand in continuity with earlier Books while still correcting the communities that carry them.

phrases.translation: The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be one of those who doubt
phrases.explanation: Truth has come from your Lord settles the source before the warning against being among doubters. Doubt in this setting would mean treating a confirmed report as unstable merely because opponents keep questioning it. The verse strengthens public confidence after a long chain of stories. It also teaches readers a method, namely compare, ask, and then refuse to let endless noise dissolve what evidence has established.

phrases.translation: and do not be one of those who deny Allah’s signs or you will be one of the losers
phrases.explanation: Do not be among those who deny Allah signs continues the command from the previous verse and attaches loss to denial. Signs include revelation, creation, history, rescue, and judgment, all woven through the chapter. Losers are people who trade that accumulated evidence for a temporary position among deniers. The short warning turns a discussion about earlier scriptures into a present choice for every hearer.

phrases.translation: Indeed, those against whom Allah’s decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will not believe—
phrases.explanation: Those against whom the word of the Lord has become justified will not believe describes a settled end after persistent rejection. Word here is a decree whose justice rests on the record that precedes it. The statement is closer to a diagnosis of hardened people in the argument than a licence to label individuals whose future remains hidden from us. It consoles the Prophet when effort meets a wall.

phrases.translation: even if every sign were to come to them—until they see the painful punishment
phrases.explanation: Even if every sign came, belief would wait until painful punishment is seen, which repeats Pharaoh problem in general form. Quantity of evidence cannot by itself heal a will committed to resistance. At the sight of punishment the issue is no longer whether the warning was real. The verse separates recognition under force from faith chosen while obedience could still shape a life.

phrases.translation: If only there had been a society which believed ˹before seeing the torment˺ and, therefore, benefited from its belief, like the people of Jonah.
phrases.explanation: Why was there no town that believed and benefited, except the people of Jonah, turns the chapter name into a bright exception. A whole community turned when punishment approached yet before it finally seized them, according to the story alluded to here. Their belief profited them because collective repentance arrived while the door of worldly rescue remained open. The exception prevents the preceding verses from becoming despair.

phrases.translation: When they believed, We lifted from them the torment of disgrace in this world and allowed them enjoyment for a while
phrases.explanation: When they believed, disgraceful punishment in this world was lifted and enjoyment was granted for a time. Nineveh in the familiar account shows that a warned city can change its ending through humility rather than negotiation over signs. For a while matters because worldly reprieve is not eternity. They received time to live differently, which is the proper use of every lifted disaster in this chapter.

phrases.translation: Had your Lord so willed ˹O Prophet˺, all ˹people˺ on earth would have certainly believed, every single one of them!
phrases.explanation: Had your Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed together places universal faith inside divine power while explaining why it is not the chosen order. Human beings are tested through response rather than manufactured as uniform believers. The verse consoles the Prophet grief over rejection by locating the limit in wisdom, not in a failure of his delivery or sincerity.

phrases.translation: Would you then force people to become believers
phrases.explanation: Will you compel people until they become believers rejects forced faith as the solution to that grief. Compulsion can produce attendance, vocabulary, and public conformity, yet it cannot manufacture the trust named belief. The question protects the inner nature of faith while leaving preaching, argument, and warning in place. A messenger may invite with urgency and still refuse to own another person conscience.

phrases.translation: It is not for any soul to believe except by Allah’s leave, and He will bring His wrath upon those who are unmindful
phrases.explanation: No soul believes except by Allah leave joins divine permission with the rejection of compulsion. Faith is a gift opened within a person, not a product squeezed out by a preacher. uncleanness or wrath falling on those who do not use reason, as early readings render the key term in related senses, warns people who refuse reflection. Permission does not erase responsibility, because unused intellect becomes part of the record.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Consider all that is in the heavens and the earth!”
phrases.explanation: Consider what is in heavens and earth sends the audience back to the evidence that opened the chapter. Sun, moon, night, sea, rain, crops, bodies, and ruins form a library available without admission fees. Consider demands more than glancing. It asks a person to stay with an object long enough for dependence, order, and purpose to become difficult to dismiss as accident.

phrases.translation: Yet neither signs nor warners are of any benefit to those who refuse to believe
phrases.explanation: Signs and warners do not benefit a people who will not believe identifies reception as the missing step. A sign can be public and a warner sincere while the audience treats both as entertainment or threat management. Benefit is not automatic exposure. The verse balances the invitation to look with honesty about why looking so often fails, returning responsibility to the eyes and heart brought to the evidence.

phrases.translation: Are they waiting for ˹anything˺ except the same torments that befell those before them?
phrases.explanation: Are they waiting except for days like those who passed before them asks whether destruction is the only teacher left. Days in this idiom are famous turns of fortune in which nations meet the outcome of their choices. Pharaoh, Noah people, and ruined towns have already supplied the curriculum. To wait for a personal edition of the same lesson is an expensive theory of education.

phrases.translation: Say, “Keep waiting then! I too am waiting with you.”
phrases.explanation: Keep waiting, I am waiting with you gives the Prophet a calm final posture rather than a threat he must personally enforce. Both sides face a future already moving toward disclosure, yet they wait with opposite expectations. The repetition echoes verse twenty and closes the sign demanding section. Patience becomes strength when a messenger refuses to purchase belief through spectacle, panic, or force.

phrases.translation: Then We saved Our messengers and those who believed. For it is Our duty to save the believers
phrases.explanation: Then We save Our messengers and believers states the rescue pattern after the waiting ends. Noah in the Ark, Moses at the sea, and believers hidden under tyranny all belong to the same promise. It is a duty upon Us expresses grace Allah has bound Himself to by promise, not an obligation imposed by anyone else. The verse gives history a hopeful grammar for minorities under pressure.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity! If you are in doubt of my faith,
phrases.explanation: O humanity opens the final declaration to everyone rather than to one tribe in Mecca. If you are in doubt about my religion invites inspection of the Prophet actual worship instead of rumours about ambition or magic. Doubt can be answered by a clear public statement of allegiance. The verse begins a short creed in which refusal, worship, death, command, and uprightness follow in order.

phrases.translation: then ˹know that˺ I do not worship those ˹idols˺ you worship instead of Allah.
phrases.explanation: I do not worship what you worship besides Allah draws the boundary without negotiation. The statement addresses idols and every being given a share in devotion, answering the proposed edits and compromises running through the chapter. A clear no is sometimes the kindest form of clarity because it stops false hope. His public identity is not for sale to a coalition of customs.

phrases.translation: But I worship Allah, Who has the power to cause your death.
phrases.explanation: But I worship Allah who will cause you to die chooses a description suited to the audience denial of return. The God he worships already holds the end they keep postponing in argument. Death is not introduced as a threat from the Prophet hand. It is named as the appointment through which every listener will meet the Lord whose worship they debate.

phrases.translation: And I have been commanded, ‘Be one of the believers,’
phrases.explanation: Commanded to be among the believers places the Prophet inside the community of faith rather than above its duties. The one who announces the boundary must live inside it first. Believers as a named group gathers Noah, Moses followers, the people of Jonah who turned, and the new audience into one moral family. Command and belonging soften the refusal with shared submission.

phrases.translation: and, ‘Be steadfast in faith in all uprightness, and do not be one of the polytheists,’
phrases.explanation: Set your face to the religion uprightly and do not be among the polytheists gives direction and boundary in one command. Face suggests full orientation of attention, worship, and life, while upright or hunafa in the classical vocabulary means inclining away from crooked association toward pure devotion. The verse is a compass sentence. A person is known by the direction repeatedly faced when loyalties compete.

phrases.translation: and ‘Do not invoke, instead of Allah, what can neither benefit nor harm you—
phrases.explanation: Do not call besides Allah on what neither benefits nor harms returns to the failed intercessor test in the most personal form. Invocation is worship in action, since the one called in ultimate need receives the heart trust. A powerless object cannot become useful through sincere tone or ancient family habit. The command protects prayer from being split among addresses that cannot answer.

phrases.translation: for if you do, then you will certainly be one of the wrongdoers,’
phrases.explanation: If you do that you will be among the wrongdoers makes even the Prophet addressee of the universal rule in form, while the warning teaches every reader. Wrongdoing includes putting devotion in the wrong place, a definition that fits association exactly. No status creates an exception to the direction of worship. The sentence is severe because a small shift in ultimate dependence changes the whole map of life.

phrases.translation: and ‘If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him.
phrases.explanation: If Allah touches you with harm, none can remove it except Him teaches where relief finally rests during illness, loss, and danger. Human means remain part of life, yet no doctor, ruler, idol, or plan can override a decree by independent power. Touch is a modest word for experiences that feel enormous from inside. The verse trains the sufferer to seek means without worshipping them.

phrases.translation: And if He intends good for you, none can withhold His bounty.
phrases.explanation: If He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty answers fear from the opposite side. Enemies, scarcity, and delay cannot form a wall high enough to stop a gift Allah has chosen. This hope does not promise every desired object. It promises that real good is never hostage to the people who dislike you. Bounty arrives under sovereignty rather than public permission.

phrases.translation: He grants it to whoever He wills of His servants.
phrases.explanation: He strikes with it or grants it to whom He wills among His servants in the translation sense of bestowing, preserving divine freedom inside generosity. Servants reminds recipients that bounty does not turn them into owners of heaven. Differences in provision therefore require humility rather than a simple ranking of worth. A gift can be a test of gratitude just as a hardship is a test of patience.

phrases.translation: And He is the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.’”
phrases.explanation: All Forgiving and Most Merciful close a hard statement about harm and bounty with the character of the One who decrees both. Forgiveness keeps the sufferer from interpreting every pain as final rejection, while mercy invites return after wrongly directed calls. The final names soften without weakening the doctrine. The same Lord who alone removes harm also wants repentant servants to approach without despair.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity! The truth has surely come to you from your Lord.
phrases.explanation: Truth has come to you from your Lord restates arrival as a completed gift at the end of the chapter. O humanity makes the closing invitation as wide as the opening letters and signs. By this point the truth includes creation, resurrection, stories, warnings, rescue, and the refusal of compulsion. What remains is not more spectacle but the decision each hearer makes with what has come.

phrases.translation: So whoever chooses to be guided, it is only for their own good.
phrases.explanation: Whoever is guided benefits his own soul places profit in the right account. Guidance does not increase Allah kingdom or pay the Prophet a wage. It rescues the guided person from a brief life spent facing the wrong direction. This framing can make obedience feel less like a favour done for religion and more like accepting medicine whose health will be experienced personally.

phrases.translation: And whoever chooses to stray, it is only to their own loss.
phrases.explanation: Whoever strays harms only himself in the ultimate account, even when his choices also injure neighbours in history. Straying may gather crowds and institutions, yet the final loss returns to the soul that chose the road. The symmetry is morally clarifying because neither acceptance nor rejection changes God. Human beings are trading with their own futures every time they answer an invitation.

phrases.translation: And I am not a keeper over you.”
phrases.explanation: I am not a keeper over you ends the Prophet role at delivery, witness, and example rather than custody of outcomes. A keeper might force, monitor, or guarantee every movement, none of which belongs to sincere faith as described in verse ninety nine. The sentence gives the audience dignity and responsibility at once. It also gives the messenger peace, because rejection cannot be converted into his failure.

phrases.translation: And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah passes His judgment.
phrases.explanation: Follow what is revealed and be patient until Allah judges gives the Prophet the last task after other people choices are released. Following keeps his road straight when audiences edit, mock, demand signs, or stall. Patience stretches that following across time, because judgment may not arrive on the timetable of insult or grief. The verse turns endurance into active obedience rather than silent waiting in a corner.

phrases.translation: For He is the Best of Judges
phrases.explanation: He is the Best of Judges closes the chapter with confidence in the final court. Human judgments have been faulty throughout, from calling truth magic to praising wealth and editing revelation. Best means perfect knowledge joined with perfect fairness and power to settle what courts and crowds leave tangled. The story can end without every dispute solved publicly because the right Judge still remains.
